Sensitivity is asserted across every kind of change the surface admits -- a version bump, an added method, a removed resource type, and the same name moving between the method and event kinds -- rather than on one representative edit. PAIRED CONTROL: an edit changing no wire-visible field leaves the fingerprint alone, so the sensitivity cases measure the CHANGE and not the act of editing; without it, a fingerprint over the whole source text would satisfy every case above while being useless. The length-prefixing case is here because of BLOCKED-085: the original case for it moved the separator CHARACTER, and removing length-prefixing reddened nothing; the replacement moves the field BOUNDARY ('ab'+'c' against 'a'+'bc', identical unprefixed) and the same mutation now reddens exactly it.

coveredBy.title: contract: a complete negotiation reaches the caller with every field intact
contract: a partially-formed negotiation is dropped WHOLE, not read field by field
contract: a server that sends no negotiation is admitted, and the field is absent rather than empty
provider: the package exports every negotiation function a peer needs

entries.note: acceptance[4]: 'the negotiated result is written to each Run's provenance.' The outcome is returned from initialize as structured provenance -- agreed version, agreed capabilities, ignored capabilities, downgrades -- so 'what did these peers agree to' is answerable from the record rather than by replaying a handshake that no longer exists. Two failure modes are closed rather than one: a partially-formed negotiation is dropped WHOLE, because a caller would treat the fields that did arrive as authoritative and a half-recorded agreement is worse than none; and an ABSENT negotiation stays absent rather than becoming an empty one, since absence means the peer predates negotiation while an empty record would assert agreement to nothing. The P-stage export case is included because provenance that no consumer can construct is not provenance: before that stage the negotiation functions existed and nothing re-exported them.

coveredBy.title: refuses the old holder's token after the item is reclaimed at a higher epoch
admits the new holder's token against the same reclaimed lease
refuses the old token after reclaim, and admits the new one
refuses the previous holder after the item is reclaimed
fault boundary 15 a delayed packet from a reclaimed holder is refused on arrival
fault boundary 16 split brain: two holders across a reclaim, only the later one writes

entries.note: acceptance[0]: 'a recovered old worker can neither submit results nor perform new side effects.' Covered through the full sequence rather than a hand-built stale token: the lease expires, the scheduler reclaims at a higher epoch, and only then does the old holder present the token it still believes is valid. The U-stage case carries it to a real state WRITE -- the fenced dispatch entry refuses to advance a lifecycle -- which is what makes 'cannot perform a side effect' more than a property of a pure comparison. Each stage's positive control sits beside its refusal, so none of these is satisfied by a check that refuses everything. NOT fully closed: the unfenced advanceAgentLifecycle export remains reachable, pinned by the U/F characterization cases rather than by a lock, because a failing case is already watching it.

coveredBy.title: decides staleness without consulting any clock, so skewed workers agree
holds the lease AT its expiry instant, so renew and reclaim cannot both be legal
extends the deadline without issuing a new epoch
refuses to renew an ALREADY-EXPIRED lease, rather than resurrecting it
fault boundary 07 a lease is still held AT its expiry instant
fault boundary 08 a lease one millisecond past expiry is reclaimable

entries.note: acceptance[1]: 'clock skew within tolerance does not produce two masters.' Satisfied by construction rather than by tuning a tolerance, and the coverage reflects that: the staleness test reads epochs only, so the C-stage case drives the same stale token against leases whose deadlines differ by the full safe-integer range and gets one verdict every time. Two workers with arbitrarily skewed clocks therefore cannot disagree about who holds authority. The remaining two-masters window is the expiry BOUNDARY, and it is pinned from both sides: a lease is still held at its expiry instant, and reclaimable one millisecond later. Renewal of an already-expired lease is refused for the same reason -- reviving a lapsed holder IS the two-masters state, since the scheduler may already have handed that item to someone else.

coveredBy.title: refuses acquisition with a reason distinct from a free item
refuses renewal while unavailable, so a holder cannot extend blindly
offers nothing reclaimable while unavailable, even for a lapsed lease
resumes normally once the store is available again
fault boundary 12 an unavailable store refuses acquisition instead of reporting the item free
fault boundary 13 an unavailable store offers nothing reclaimable
fault boundary 14 an unavailable store refuses renewal

entries.note: acceptance[2]: 'stop taking new work when the lease store fails.' Stop-work is proved in BOTH directions -- nothing can be acquired and nothing is offered as reclaimable -- because a scheduler blocked on one path and fed by the other would still start work. The refusal carries a DISTINCT 'store-unavailable' tag rather than a null or empty result: 'nobody holds this' and 'I cannot tell you who holds this' must not look alike, since reporting an item free during an outage is exactly how the same work item reaches a second worker. The fourth case is a positive control and is load-bearing here -- without it, a store stuck permanently unavailable would satisfy every one of the refusal cases above.

coveredBy.title: acceptance[0]: the offline cold start is the same call, with no network-shaped parameter
admits an install that matches the lock exactly, and returns the locked order
admits a matching install and reports the boot as verified
fault boundary 15 boot refuses a locked plugin missing from disk (validation[2])

entries.note: acceptance[0]: 'an offline cold start can verify the local cache against the lock.' Satisfied structurally rather than by an offline test harness: every input to admitBoot is already-resolved data -- the lock's facts and the installed facts -- with no registry handle, URL, or process handle anywhere in the parameter list. There is therefore no network path to omit when the network is gone, so the offline call and the online call are THE SAME call and cannot diverge. The F-stage boundary covers the other half: a cache missing a locked plugin is refused rather than silently booting short.

coveredBy.title: reports drift when the registry has moved, without changing what boot loads
refuses the drifted version even once it is what is installed
fault boundary 13 boot refuses a version drift ahead of the digests it would also fail

entries.note: acceptance[1]: 'registry tag drift does not change an already-locked profile.' Covered from both directions, which is what the clause needs. Detecting drift is reported and nothing else happens -- following the registry is precisely what a lock exists to prevent, so the only legitimate response is to tell someone. And once the drifted version is what is actually INSTALLED, boot refuses it: a lock that reported drift but then loaded the new version would be a lock in name only. The F boundary pins that this refusal reports version-mismatch rather than the integrity mismatch it would also fail, so an operator is told a different version is installed rather than that the package was tampered with.

coveredBy.title: acceptance[2]: refuses a candidate generated from a lock that has since changed
reports the candidate defect even when the base ALSO moved
replaces an existing lock with the new content
leaves no scratch file behind, so a reader never finds a partial lock
writes a complete, re-readable lock when the target did not exist

entries.note: acceptance[2]: 'two concurrent install processes do not produce a half-written lock.' Covered in two independent senses, and the second is only PARTLY closed -- stated here rather than left for a reader to discover. (a) Logical: a candidate generated from a base that has since moved is refused, so two installs that both read version 3 cannot each silently erase the other's work. (b) Physical: replacement goes through a sibling temp file and a rename, and the cases prove the content lands whole with no scratch file surviving. They do NOT prove atomicity -- that is a property of rename(2), and observing a partial write would need a reader racing the writer; replacing temp-and-rename with an in-place write reddens none of them. Recorded in the P-stage freeze, the suite's module comment, and the package README rather than closed with an assertion that a function was called.

coveredBy.title: refuses a derived record naming no source event
accepts a user-asserted record, which names a responsible party instead
does not treat an empty asserter as traceable
fault boundary 09 validation[0] source deletion: a derived record left with no sources is refused
fault boundary 10 validation[0] source deletion: a user-asserted record survives it

entries.note: acceptance[0]: 'every memory traces to at least one source, or is explicitly marked user-asserted.' Enforced structurally rather than by a check that could be bypassed: the two origins are separate VARIANTS of MemoryProvenance, so a derived record with an empty source list is refused by validateRecord and there is no third state. That split is what keeps 'nobody recorded where this came from' from reading as 'the user said so' -- with one possibly-empty list the two would be the same value. The F boundaries carry it under source deletion specifically, from both sides: deleting the last source event refuses the record rather than silently downgrading it, while a user-asserted record has no sources to lose. An empty asserter string is also not traceable, so the user-asserted variant cannot be used as an empty escape hatch.

coveredBy.title: retrieves an active, unexpired record
withholds a record whose validity has passed, and keeps one at the boundary out too
withholds revoked, superseded and disputed records alike
fault boundary 07 validation[0] time validity: a record is retrievable up to, but not at, its end
fault boundary 15 a revoked record is withheld even while still within its validity

entries.note: acceptance[1]: 'expired and revoked records do not enter default retrieval.' Covered on both axes, because the two exclusions are independent -- a record can be revoked while still within its validity window, and boundary 15 pins exactly that. The time axis is pinned at the instant: retrievable at 23:59:59.999 and withheld at the end instant itself, since at the moment validity ends the claim is no longer true. `disputed` is withheld too, which is the judgement worth recording: a disputed record's claim is not known to be false, but returning it by DEFAULT would present a contested fact as settled, and a caller who wants it can ask explicitly.

coveredBy.title: permits it and reports that no boundary was crossed
refuses a cross-tenant merge with no authorization
refuses a cross-session merge with a DIFFERENT reason from a cross-tenant one
permits a cross-tenant merge that names both endpoints
refuses an authorization issued for a different destination
refuses an authorization issued for a different source
does not let a session-scoped authorization cover a tenant-wide merge

entries.note: acceptance[2]: 'a merge across scopes must be explicit.' The authorization names BOTH endpoints, and three of these cases exist for that alone -- one naming only the destination would authorize merging into it from anywhere, so a single approval would cover every later merge. A same-scope merge is permitted and reports crossesScope: false, so an audit can distinguish the two without re-deriving it. Tenant and session crossings refuse with different reasons because they are events of different severity: one moves data between customers, the other within one. NOT COVERED HERE, deliberately: whether a RUNTIME enforces this on real reads. decideCrossScopeMerge is a decision, and the runtime that would consult it is P6-01's MemoryRuntime, whose scope post-filtering is the residual lock now owned by P6-03 (BLOCKED-096).

coveredBy.title: resumes at the first step that is not skippable, not past it
does not repeat a completed child agent call: its receipt is retained and its step skipped
kill BEFORE the agent call settles: the step is re-run
kill AFTER the agent call settles but before verification: still re-run
kill after verification: the completed child work is NOT repeated
kill between two agent calls: the finished one is skipped, the next re-run
kill during concurrent calls started out of order: the journal still reads in script order

entries.note: acceptance[0]: 'kill before and after each agent() call; the resume does not repeat completed child work.' Covered at three levels rather than once, because the clause is about a SEQUENCE and each level can be right while the next is wrong. C decides one entry; P drives the recorder through the three kill points a real session produces (before settle, after settle but before verification, after verification) and checks the plan each yields; U drives the same through the host's actual agent event stream, including concurrent out-of-order starts. The middle kill point is the one that matters most and is easiest to miss: a step that settled but was never verified is re-run, because 'it finished' and 'we checked it' are different facts.

coveredBy.title: refuses the WHOLE resume rather than degrading to a partial one
admits an unchanged digest, so the refusal is not unconditional
fault boundary 09 a changed script digest refuses the whole resume
fault boundary 14 a refused plan yields no receipts to reconcile

entries.note: acceptance[1]: 'a changed script digest must not be blindly resumed; migrate or restart.' The refusal is whole rather than partial: step ids are positions in a script, so against a different script they name different work, and a partial resume would skip steps never run while re-running steps that were. Boundary 14 covers the consequence a caller could otherwise miss -- a refused plan yields NO receipts, so a caller cannot reconcile its way into acting on a journal the system just refused. The positive control (an unchanged digest is admitted) is load-bearing: without it a function refusing every resume would satisfy the rest.

coveredBy.title: drops recomputable inputs from a completed, verified, pure step
leaves an unverified or side-effecting step untouched
retains EVERY receipt, which is the evidence nothing can regenerate
reports a compaction that dropped a receipt as NOT retaining evidence
fault boundary 16 compaction retains every receipt
fault boundary 17 compacting an already-compacted journal changes nothing further

entries.note: acceptance[2]: 'a journal may be compacted but the raw evidence is retained.' Compaction drops what can be recomputed (a pure verified step's input refs, derivable from the steps that produced them) and keeps what cannot -- every receipt, from every entry, because a receipt is evidence that something happened OUTSIDE this process and nothing inside it can regenerate that. retainsAllReceipts is EXPORTED so the property is checkable by a caller rather than only by this package's tests, and one case asserts it reports FALSE for a compaction that dropped a receipt -- without that control, its returning true would prove nothing. Boundary 17 adds idempotence, which the clause does not name: a journal compacted at every checkpoint must not shed more information each pass.

coveredBy.title: treats a body containing executable-looking text as opaque data
stores and resolves a definition whose body would throw if evaluated
fault boundary 18 acceptance[0]: a hostile body registers and resolves without executing

entries.note: acceptance[0]: 'saving and loading never executes unverified code.' Demonstrated rather than asserted: the cases register and resolve a definition whose body is `process.exit(1); throw new Error("executed")`. If any path evaluated a body, the test process would die or the case would throw. The property is structural underneath -- `body` is typed `string` and every function that touches it either hashes it or pattern-matches it, so there is no evaluator to reach. declaresNestedCall is deliberately textual for the same reason; parsing would mean building the evaluator this clause forbids, and over-reporting is the safe direction since a false positive refuses a registration a human then inspects.

coveredBy.title: propagates to the child

entries.note: acceptance[1]: 'a parent's cancellation propagates.' Covered at the DECISION level only, and the limit is the point: cancelPropagationForNested() states that a nested child is cancelled with its parent, and a case pins it. Nothing propagates a real cancellation, because nothing starts a nested run -- see acceptance[3]'s note and the U-stage tripwire. The decision exists so that when nesting is wired, the answer is already written down rather than improvised by whoever wires it; it is not evidence that a running parent cancels a running child.

coveredBy.title: fails the parent when the policy says so
continues the parent but still RECORDS the failure

entries.note: acceptance[2]: 'a child failure is handled by the declared policy.' Both branches are covered, and the second carries the substance: `continue-parent` still RECORDS the failure. A policy that let a parent ignore a failed child would make that child's work indistinguishable from work that never ran, and a parent reporting success while a declared child failed silently is exactly what this clause exists to prevent. Same decision-level limit as acceptance[1].

coveredBy.title: refuses at the depth ceiling, and admits one step below it
refuses when the agent or token budget is spent
gives the child what remains, minus the call that started it
caps the child at its decayed agent budget, not at the deployment ceiling
fault boundary 13 the depth ceiling admits one below and refuses at it
fault boundary 15 the last remaining agent may still be spent on a nested run
fault boundary 12 recursion is detected anywhere on the ancestor chain, not only at the parent

entries.note:
acceptance[3]: 'recursion depth, total agents and total budget are bounded.' Each ceiling is pinned from BOTH sides -- admitted one step below, refused at it -- because a limit tested only from the refusing side is satisfied by a check that refuses everything. The decay is what makes the totals hold: a child receives what remains minus the call that started it, so a tree cannot have every run believe it holds the full allowance. Recursion is refused structurally and anywhere on the chain, not merely caught by depth, so an operator learns 'this definition calls itself' rather than 'this got too deep'.

must[3] IS NOT CLAIMED AS COVERED, per the delegate's ruling. The clause is about the RUNTIME behaviour of nested workflows, and `runtime.ts` installs no `workflow()` global, so a script cannot start one and nothing can violate the clause today. The vacuum is held by a mutation-proved tripwire in the U stage rather than by prose: it fails the day a nesting hook appears, forcing whoever adds it to face must[3] then. These entries cover the DECISIONS a future wiring will consult; they do not cover a running worker enforcing them.
